Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14253746/assets/dbf36192ac332dc49ed75278838e989a37ac7d888311be1b8b059a7b59667aa6.png)

Let's first find the value of angle $2\theta +\frac{\pi }{2}$ where $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3}.$

$$
2\theta +\frac{\pi }{2}=2(\frac{\pi }{3})+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{7\pi }{6}.
$$

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{7\pi }{6}$ corresponds to the point $(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},-\frac{1}{2}).$ Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6})=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$

Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6})=-\frac{1}{2}.$ 

Using the fact that $\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }$ and $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6}) & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6})}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6})}=\frac{(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}{(-\frac{1}{2})}=\sqrt{3}, \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6}) & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6})}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6})}=\frac{(-\frac{1}{2})}{(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we combine the results:

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡(2\theta +\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{tan}⁡(2\theta +\frac{\pi }{2})=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6})+\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6})=\sqrt{3}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}=\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{3}.
$$
